video_title: How a Small Spice Company Beat Trump’s Tariffs | Ethan Frisch
gist: ChinaTalk interviews Ethan Frisch of spice importer Burlap and Barrel, a plaintiff in suits against the Section 122 and Section 301 tariffs, with Peter Peter explaining the legal fallback after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs. Covers 301 litigation odds, 12-18 month appeal timeline, refunds, small-importer tariff economics and why big firms stay out.

insights.claim: After the Supreme Court ruled in February that the IEEPA tariffs were illegal in the Learning Resources case, the administration did not abandon tariffs but substituted a two-step fallback: Section 122 tariffs for 150 days, then Section 301 tariffs imposed in July.
insights.speaker: Peter
insights.so_what: Court losses have not reduced the effective tariff wall; the legal basis keeps rotating, so headline rulings overstate relief for importers.

insights.claim: The Section 301 tariffs rest on USTR findings that about 60 jurisdictions (including the EU) fail to prohibit imports of forced-labor goods, and they cover jurisdictions accounting for roughly 99% of US trade at 10% or 12.5%.
insights.speaker: Peter
insights.so_what: Near-universal baseline tariff persists through a new statute; baseline-rate exposure for importers is not going away on the strength of the IEEPA ruling alone.

insights.claim: The 301 rate structure is 10% if a country has a forced-labor import ban it fails to enforce and 12.5% if it has no ban, and China, widely seen as the worst forced-labor offender, gets 12.5% like roughly two-thirds of other countries, so rates do not track forced-labor severity.
insights.speaker: Peter
insights.so_what: Undifferentiated rates undercut the stated statutory rationale and strengthen the pretext argument at the Court of International Trade.
insights.quote: China has a 12% tariff. China's probably the biggest forced labor problem in the world.

insights.claim: Rates and product exemptions under 301 largely replicate those the Supreme Court struck down in February, and Trump said on the afternoon of the loss that other authorities would be used to recreate the tariffs, which the plaintiffs treat as evidence of pretext.
insights.speaker: Peter
insights.so_what: Administration intent is documented, so pretext arguments carry weight; expect continued statute-hopping.
insights.quote: Both the tariff rates and the exemptions largely track the tariff rates that the Supreme Court ruled illegal

insights.claim: Section 301 has been used about 130 times, including Trump's first-term China tariffs, but always as a targeted, negotiating-leverage tool against a discrete unfair practice of one country; using it for permanent, near-global tariffs is a fundamentally different application.
insights.speaker: Peter
insights.so_what: The core legal vulnerability is scope and breadth, not the existence of 301 authority.

insights.claim: The government's litigation posture leans on judicial deference to executive interpretation, and Ethan Frisch argues its case is weak because 301 has never been applied so sweepingly and the 301 tariffs are a copy-paste of the 122 and IEEPA structure with a new justification.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: If courts reject deference, the whole country-tariff architecture is exposed.

insights.claim: At the Court of International Trade hearing the day before, a three-judge panel appeared skeptical of the government, and Frisch expects to win at least this first round, as he did in the Section 122 case.
insights.speaker: Peter
insights.so_what: Lower-court win is probable but, per the speakers, largely non-binding on cash flows given appeal practice.

insights.claim: Even a Court of International Trade win will be appealed to the Federal Circuit and almost certainly the Supreme Court, with an expected 12 to 18 months before final resolution.
insights.speaker: Peter
insights.so_what: Tariff uncertainty for importers is a roughly year-and-a-half problem; do not assume near-term removal.

insights.claim: In prior tariff litigation, courts deferred to the government by letting it keep collecting tariffs during appeals even after ruling against it on the merits, so importers keep paying until final judgment and only get refunds if they ultimately prevail.
insights.speaker: Peter
insights.so_what: Refund claims are a contingent asset that ties up importer cash for a long time.
insights.quote: the government is going to be able to continue collecting the tariffs uh during the appeals

insights.claim: Burlap and Barrel received its IEEPA tariff refund from customs a few weeks earlier, a sub-six-figure sum with interest of roughly 3.5%.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: IEEPA refunds are actually being paid, with interest, which supports positioning around refund claims; amounts for large importers could be material.

insights.claim: Tariffs are pulled by direct debit from importers' bank accounts with no opportunity to negotiate rates, unlike haggling over a rate.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Collection is automatic and efficient while refunds are slow, an asymmetry that pressures small-business cash flow.

insights.claim: The 122 tariffs started the same day the earlier set ended and Frisch is also a plaintiff in the 122 suit, which is still being litigated though the tariffs have lapsed; he says money is owed back to companies.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Section 122 refund claims are a further pool of potential refunds.

themes.theme: Who sues and why big companies sit out

insights.claim: Plaintiffs in the tariff cases have been small businesses (Learning Resources, Burlap and Barrel) and Democratic-led states such as Oregon, New York and California, while large companies paying billions in tariffs have stayed on the sidelines out of fear of retaliation.
insights.speaker: Peter
insights.so_what: Large importers free-ride on small plaintiffs and will still collect refunds; their absence is a behavioral signal about perceived political risk.
insights.quote: you would ordinarily expect to kind of be the lead plaintiffs on this sort of thing because they're paying billions in tariffs have just been sitting on the sidelines

insights.claim: Neither Peter nor Frisch have seen retaliation from USTR, CBP or Justice Department lawyers against tariff plaintiffs, only rhetoric in aggregate; Peter suggests professionalism of those agencies and judges watching may explain it, even though retaliation has occurred in other policy areas.
insights.speaker: Peter
insights.so_what: The fear premium keeping large firms out of litigation may be overstated, which could lead to more corporate plaintiffs later.

insights.claim: Frisch judged the retaliation risk acceptable because the company has no outside investors, the founders own 100%, and the business benefits from earned media, whereas companies with boards and investors face more hurdles to joining.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Governance structure predicts who will litigate against the government.

insights.claim: The tariff suits are being run pro bono by the libertarian Liberty Justice Center in Chicago, which approached Burlap and Barrel after it filed an amicus brief in the district court case.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Pro bono activist litigation lowers the cost barrier for small plaintiffs and sustains the case pipeline.

insights.claim: Spice tariffs hit Burlap and Barrel only modestly because duties apply to bulk raw product, the spice itself is a small fraction of unit costs, and the largest cost in the chain is shipping from warehouse to the customer's home.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Importers of bulk inputs with heavy downstream value-add are far less tariff-sensitive than importers of finished goods like iPhones.

insights.claim: The company paid tariffs of generally 10 to 20% on bulk cost depending on the daily rate on arrival, for example about 10% on black pepper bought at roughly $15 per kilo in Zanzibar, with 5 to 10 tons imported per year.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete tariff-per-unit scale for a small food importer.

insights.claim: The main tariff impact was cash flow: as a bootstrapped company paying large deposits to farmers before receiving product, it had tight moments in its bank account, but sales still grew.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: For small importers tariffs bite through working capital rather than margin.

insights.claim: After Liberation Day the company ran a tariff sale, pledged not to raise consumer prices or cut payments to farmers, and a viral social post produced about a quarter-million dollars of sales in a short time.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Small DTC brands can convert tariff news into demand, so tariff headline shocks are not purely negative for them.

insights.claim: Frisch says the company is doing well in this environment and that tariff-related press and litigation have helped the business, even though he calls the tariffs illegal overreach.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Earned media from tariff activism is a real, if idiosyncratic, offset for small brands.

insights.claim: When the company emailed customers about suing the president, positive and negative replies came back in almost equal numbers (about a hundred each), most negative ones from non-customers, and overall business was up.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Political stances showed little measurable sales cost for a premium DTC brand.
insights.quote: almost exactly the same number of positive and negative emails back

insights.claim: Frisch says direct-to-consumer interactions show inflation and economic downturn as a much bigger obstacle for small businesses than the tariffs themselves, with consumers cutting discretionary food purchases and being more careful.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Anecdotal evidence of weak discretionary spending among consumers in late 2026.

insights.claim: Large companies weather tariffs better because of the cash moving through their systems at scale, while small businesses focus on micro-margin questions like covering tariff costs and keeping customers buying.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Tariffs favor scale players and squeeze small competitors.

insights.claim: Frisch says American consumers do not care about ethical sourcing or supply chains and just want spices that taste good, so the company centers marketing on flavor rather than its social-enterprise story.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Ethics-led brand positioning is a weak demand driver; product quality sells.
insights.quote: They don't care about good good supply chains.

themes.theme: Burlap and Barrel business model and sourcing

insights.claim: Burlap and Barrel is about 70% direct-to-consumer through its own site, expects close to 150,000 orders in 2026, imports from about 28 countries, and also sells to grocery, restaurants, artisan manufacturers and Amazon.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Sizing for a bootstrapped specialty food DTC brand.

insights.claim: Single-origin sourcing from small farmers gives fresher and distinct varieties, with the warehouse turning over annually versus supermarket spices that are already about three years old at purchase.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Quality differentiation versus incumbent mass-market spice brands is the core competitive claim.

insights.claim: The company pays what farmers ask ('farmer pricing') because spice is a small share of unit cost; an extra dollar per kilo is trivial to the company but material to the farmer, and it describes this as a long-term-relationship approach.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Low input-cost share lets premium brands absorb supplier price increases and tariffs more easily.
insights.quote: we pay farmers whatever they ask we call it farmer pricing

insights.claim: Market access has scaled suppliers: a Zanzibar black pepper co-op went from a few hundred kilos to at least five tons a year sold to the company, and Royal Cinnamon from Vietnam is its bestselling product.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Demand-side pull from specialty importers can scale smallholder supply.

insights.claim: Most spices like black pepper, cinnamon and vanilla cannot be grown in the US, so tariffs on them do not protect domestic production, whereas garlic has long been tariffed because of California growers.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Tariffs on non-producible commodities are pure cost with no import-substitution upside.
insights.quote: Most spices don't grow in the US.

insights.claim: Because spices are a small, low-volume grocery category, the company is diversifying into single-origin sugars, wild-harvested honey from Tanzania, pomegranate molasses and familiar blends, with blends the most successful line in the past year.
insights.speaker: Ethan
insights.so_what: Specialty food brands pivot to accessible blends and adjacent pantry categories to grow beyond a niche.

insights.claim: Peter argues policy circles underappreciate that courts may strike down all the country-level tariffs (steel tariffs rest on other authorities), so the assumption that the next president inherits them could be wrong, and the courts rather than the executive may decide long-term tariff policy.
insights.speaker: Peter
insights.so_what: Long-run tariff path is a judicial risk, with downside for tariff-dependent revenue assumptions.

insights.claim: Peter expects a wide-open Democratic 2028 primary and a median Democratic president elected on affordability who removes a decent chunk of the tariffs but keeps some as leverage or industry protection.
insights.speaker: Peter
insights.so_what: Suggests partial, not full, tariff unwinding after 2028 even under a Democratic win.

insights.claim: Jordan Schneider notes Biden did not cut Trump's first-term tariffs, so reversal under a successor is not assured.
insights.speaker: Jordan Schneider
insights.so_what: Tariff stickiness across administrations is a base-rate argument against full rollback.

insights.claim: Peter and Schneider both view the forced-labor rationale as pretext, noting the forced labor prevention act (co-sponsored by Rubio) funded enforcement while the same justification is now used to tariff European goods.
insights.speaker: Peter
insights.so_what: Using forced labor as tariff window dressing may weaken real forced-labor enforcement credibility.
